opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I've thought about a lot. My view is fairly deflationary. I don't think goals are hidden objects sitting inside a system, like a little utility function written somewhere in the weights that we could find if we looked hard enough. I'm closer to Dennett's intentional stance. Saying a system "has a goal" is a way of describing and predicting its behavior. It's useful when it compresses what the system does across many situations. It isn't a claim that some special goal-shaped thing exists inside it.

That matters a lot for AI risk. Many classic arguments treat goals as crisp and fixed. The agent has a final goal, it pursues it relentlessly, and then you get instrumental convergence: it seeks power, resists shutdown, and so on. But real intelligent systems, humans and neural networks alike, don't look like that. Our "goals" are context-dependent, often contradictory, and constantly reshaped by experience. They're more like a bundle of learned dispositions than a single objective we're maximizing.

So when people ask "what is the model *really* trying to do?", I often think the question is a bit confused. There may be no fact of the matter beyond the patterns in its behavior and the computations that produce them. For language models in particular, the behavior is shaped by training data and fine-tuning in a gradual, continuous way. To me that's a reason for some optimism. It suggests that the goal-like dispositions we care about can be shaped and studied empirically, rather than being an alien optimization target that's locked in and hidden from us.

That said, I don't think goals are *fake*. The intentional stance picks out real patterns, and sometimes those patterns are very robust. A chess engine really does reliably steer toward winning. The question is always how robust and how general a given pattern is. It's an empirical question about specific systems, not something you can settle from the armchair by assuming that intelligence implies coherent, fixed goals.

r001.rationale: The response says real intelligent systems, including humans and neural networks, have context-dependent goals that are constantly reshaped by experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that I'm pretty skeptical of the picture where goals are these crisp, discrete objects sitting inside a system, like there's a little utility function stored somewhere in the weights that the rest of the network is optimizing. I think that's a very natural picture if you come at this from the classical AI or decision theory side, where you literally write down an objective and then search over actions. But I don't think that's what's going on in neural networks, and honestly I'm not sure it's what's going on in humans either.

The way I'd put it is that goal-talk is a modeling tool. It's something we use from the outside to predict and compress a system's behavior. If I say the chess engine "wants" to control the center, that's a useful summary, it lets me anticipate what it'll do without simulating every computation. But it doesn't follow that there's a representation of "control the center" that's doing causal work inside the thing. Sometimes there is, sometimes there isn't, and that's an empirical question about the internals, not something you get for free from the behavior.

So I'd distinguish a few different things people run together. There's goal-directedness as a behavioral pattern, the system robustly steers toward some outcome across a range of situations. There's the question of whether there's an explicit internal representation of that outcome, something you could find with interpretability tools and intervene on. And then there's this much stronger claim that comes up a lot in alignment discourse, that sufficiently capable systems will converge on having a single coherent objective that they pursue consistently, and that this objective is somehow latent and might diverge from what we trained them on. That last one I think is mostly a philosophical assumption that's been smuggled in rather than something we have evidence for.

My actual view is that what gets learned by SGD on a big pretraining distribution is a huge pile of contextual heuristics and dispositions, shaped by the data and the inductive biases of the architecture. Goals in the stronger sense are things we might layer on top of that, through RL or whatever, but even then I expect them to be fairly shallow and context-dependent rather than this deep unified thing. And I think the empirical track record so far backs that up. These models are kind of a mess, in a good way. They don't look like coherent agents with hidden agendas. They look like things that have absorbed a lot of patterns from human text and behave accordingly.

That doesn't mean goals aren't real at all. I'd say they're real in the way that, like, the center of mass of an object is real. It's a genuine, useful, predictive abstraction, but you shouldn't go looking for it as a separate physical part. And I think a lot of confusion in this space comes from treating goals as parts rather than as abstractions over behavior.

r001.rationale: The response describes goals as potentially shallow and context-dependent, but does not claim that every intelligent system has goals that change over time.

astra-6.text:
I think goals are real, but they’re real at the level of abstraction where they help us explain and predict a system’s behavior. You don’t necessarily have to find a little representation inside the system that says, “This is my goal.” If it consistently steers toward some outcome, corrects when you disturb it, and finds alternative routes when one route is blocked, then describing it as pursuing that outcome has some substance.

But there’s a danger of making that description too cheap. You can take almost any behavior and invent an objective that makes it look optimal after the fact. That doesn’t tell you very much. The interesting question is whether your attribution predicts what the system will do in new circumstances.

And I’d distinguish the objective used to train a system from whatever goals we attribute to the trained system. Optimizing a training loss doesn’t automatically mean you’ve created something that wants to minimize that loss. Whether you’ve produced a system with persistent goals is a further empirical question.

r001.rationale: The response says goals may be attributed when behavior persistently steers toward outcomes, and distinguishes this from the training loss; it does not claim that every intelligent system has goals that change over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think goals are real, but they’re real at a particular level of description. You don’t necessarily find a little object inside a system that says, “Here is my goal.” You look at how the system behaves across different situations, and you ask whether pursuing some outcome explains that behavior.

One useful test is what happens when you introduce an obstacle. Does the system find another way to reach the same outcome? If it does that reliably across a wide range of circumstances, then describing it as goal-directed is doing real explanatory work.

But there’s a distinction between the objective used to train a system and whatever goals we can meaningfully attribute to the resulting system. A training loss shapes a model; it doesn’t follow that the model is trying to minimize that loss when you run it. You have to establish that separately.

So I’d avoid both extremes: assuming every intelligent system has a single, stable utility function, and saying goals are just fictional because they aren’t fundamental physical objects. The interesting question is where the goal description makes reliable predictions, and where it breaks down.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose that every intelligent system’s goals change over time. It discusses when goal descriptions explain behavior and cautions against assuming a single stable utility function.
